mythology.body:
The ​stories of ‌Wiraqucha ‌place ​creator, sky, ​sea ​foam at ​the ​center ‌of a ​living ​mythological world.

### ‌Origins ​(Myth)

‌Wiraqucha appears ​in ‌incan tradition ​as ​creator, ​sky, sea ​foam. ​The name's ‌meaning, ​"Sea ‌of fat", ​shapes ‌the narratives ​told ‌about ​this figure.

### ‌Worship ​and Memory ​(Cult)

‌Devotees ‌and later ‌tradition-keepers ​preserved Wiraqucha ​in ‌ritual, ​text, and ​iconography, ‌ensuring the ​name ​survived ‌into the ​modern ‌scholarly ​record.

The ​myths ​of Wiraqucha ​survive ‌in ‌fragments, summaries, ​and ‌later retellings. ​Each ​version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of its ‌tellers ​— ‌poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and scholars. ​The ‌PuniCodex ​entry does ​not ​privilege a ‌single ​version; ​it gathers ​the ‌attestations so ​that ‌readers ​can compare ‌them. ​The restoration ‌Wiraqucha ‌gives ​the figure ​a ​stable name ​around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌Wiraqucha, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​creator ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

overview.body:
**Wiraqucha** ​(*viracocha*) — ‌Creator, Sky, ‌Sea Foam ​· Sea ​of ​fat — ​belongs to ​the Incan ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under the ​domain "Creator, ‌Sky, Sea ​Foam". The ‌name ​means "Sea ​of fat"[^1].

​**Wiraqucha** is ​the maker ​of ‌the Inca ​cosmos: sky ‌father, creator ​of sun ‌and ​moon, and ‌the weeping ​wanderer who ‌once walked ​the ​length of ‌the Andes ‌and was ‌never seen ​again. ​The chroniclers ‌knew him ​as the ​invisible god ‌who ​made the ​world and ‌then withdrew ​from it ‌— and ​his ​name still ​survives in ​the politest ‌word an ‌Andean ​elder can ‌offer a ​stranger: *wiraqucha*, ​sir, gentleman, ‌lord.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ​**Wiraqucha** and ‌serves ​its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/viracocha/). The ‌displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a description ‌computed from ​the displayed ​form ​itself. The ‌plain ASCII ​form *viracocha* ‌contains the ​same letters: ‌no ​recovered diacritics ‌or special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work ​here is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

the-name.body:
No ​indigenous written ‌attestation ‌survives for ​this name; ​**Wiraqucha** ​is a ​scholarly ​transliteration of ‌the ​reconstructed spoken ​form. ‌Etymologically the ​name means ‌"Sea ​of fat"[^1].

‌The ​canonical spelling ​**Wiraqucha** ​matches the ​conventional ​scholarly romanization. ‌The plain ​ASCII ‌form *viracocha* ​contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so no ​lost ‌diacritics or ​encoding transition ​is ‌claimed. The ‌editorial ‌work is ​to ​fix one ‌reviewed ​reference spelling, ​preserve capitalization ‌and ​provenance, and ​keep ‌the original ​evidence ‌visible. The ​displayed ​form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ‌description computed ‌from ​the displayed ‌form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

meditation.body:
Wiraqucha is ​the absent ‌creator — ‌the maker ​who finished ​his work, ​wept once ​over what ​was coming, ‌and left. ​Andean theology ​has no jealous ‌guardian and ​no returning ‌savior: the ​world was ‌handed over, ​and what ​happens in ​it is, ​up to ​a point, ‌the world's own ​business. That ‌withdrawal is ​the deepest ‌note in ​his mythology. ‌Where other ​high gods ‌demand attention, ​Wiraqucha demands ​only remembrance ‌— his name ‌spoken in ‌honorifics, his ​lake crossed ​at the ‌solstice, his ​ruined workshop ​kept as ‌pilgrimage ground.

​And the ​weeping is ‌the detail that ​keeps scholars ‌returning. A ​god who ​cries at ​a spring, ​foretelling bearded ‌men in ‌his own ​dress, is ‌a god ​who has read ​the ending ‌of the ‌story he ‌began. The ‌chronicles that ​preserve the ‌scene were ​written under ​colonial rule, ​which should ‌make us careful ​— but ​even as ​colonial construction ‌it is ​extraordinary: a ​conquered people ​explaining the ‌conquest in ​the voice ‌of their ​own god, who ‌saw it ​coming and ‌left before ‌it arrived. ​Absence, prophecy, ​grief: the ​maker's last ​gifts were ‌the ones ‌no one ​could take.[^1]
